option_description: Controls whether SIEM correlation rules are actively deployed and running against live log data in the production environment, as opposed to being merely imported, staged, or left in test/simulation mode.
security_impact: This is the foundational gate for the rule_based_detection_accuracy Rego rule. If rules_deployed_and_enabled is false, the entire rule-based detection countermeasure fails to activate regardless of tuning quality or false positive rates. Without active rules, no alerts fire, meaning known threat patterns pass through the SIEM undetected and no response orchestration can be triggered.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the SIEM management console (e.g., Splunk Enterprise Security, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, Elastic SIEM). Navigate to the detection rules or correlation search management section. Filter by rule status and confirm at least one rule set shows 'Active', 'Enabled', or 'Running' state. Verify rules are assigned to a production environment, not a sandbox or test index.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Security Content > Correlation Searches > Status column | Sentinel: Analytics > Active rules tab | QRadar: Rules > Rule Status column | Elastic: Security > Rules > Enabled toggle
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more rules in 'Active' or 'Enabled' state with last-fired timestamps within the past 24 hours.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API to retrieve the list of enabled correlation rules. Inspect the returned rule objects for an enabled/active status field.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/correlation_rules?status=enabled' | jq '[.rules[] | select(.enabled==true)] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count greater than 0 indicating at least one rule is in enabled state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk ES, use the Splunk CLI or search API to query saved searches tagged as correlation searches and check their enablement status.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches?search=action.correlationsearch.enabled%3D1&output_mode=json' | jq '.entry[] | {name: .name, enabled: .content.disabled}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output listing correlation searches where 'disabled' field is false, confirming active deployment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM's internal audit or system log for evidence of rules firing alerts within the last 24–48 hours. Absence of any fired-rule log entries alongside live data ingestion is a strong indicator that no rules are enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'correlation_rule\|rule_triggered\|alert_generated' /var/log/siem/audit.log | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing rule match events with recent timestamps, confirming active rule execution.

option_description: Captures the measured percentage of SIEM-generated alerts over the last 30 days that were determined to be false positives, calculated as (false positive alert count / total alert count) * 100. Serves as the primary tuning efficacy metric.
security_impact: The Rego policy for rule_based_detection_accuracy enforces a threshold of false_positive_rate_percent <= 20. Rates above 20% indicate that alert noise is overwhelming analyst capacity, causing genuine threats to be buried in false positives and increasing mean time to detection. High false positive rates erode analyst trust and lead to alert fatigue, effectively nullifying detection capability even when rules are technically active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SIEM or integrated ticketing system (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira, PagerDuty) and pull alert disposition reports for the last 30 days. Filter by analyst-assigned disposition of 'False Positive' and divide by total closed alert count. Many SIEMs have a built-in alert metrics or investigation dashboard showing this ratio.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Incident Review > Search last 30 days > filter by status='false_positive' | Sentinel: Incidents blade > filter Closed/False Positive > export count | QRadar: Offenses > Closed Offenses > filter by close reason 'False Positive'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A disposition breakdown showing count of False Positive vs. True Positive closures over the 30-day window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or ticketing system API for alert disposition data over a 30-day window and calculate the false positive ratio programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/alerts?start_date=$(date -d '-30 days' +%Y-%m-%d)&end_date=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)&disposition=false_positive' | jq '{fp_count: .total, query: "false_positives"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Separate counts for false positive and total alerts enabling manual or scripted ratio calculation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk ES, run a search against the notable events index to compute the false positive rate over 30 days directly in the Splunk search bar.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS -X POST 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' --data 'search=index=notable earliest=-30d | stats count(eval(status="5")) as fp_count, count as total_count | eval fp_rate=round((fp_count/total_count)*100,2)&output_mode=json'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output containing fp_rate field representing the false positive percentage for the last 30 days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC team lead or SIEM administrator to obtain the most recent false positive rate metric. Request any weekly or monthly SOC metrics reports that track alert quality. If no formal tracking exists, this is itself a finding indicating the value cannot be reliably determined.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented percentage figure from a SOC metrics report, ideally below 20%, with evidence of regular tracking.

option_description: Represents the degree to which SIEM correlation rules have been customized to the specific production environment, including configuration of allowlists for known-good activity, threshold adjustments based on observed baselines, suppression of acknowledged noise sources, and behavioral deviation alert calibration.
security_impact: The Rego policy requires rule_tuning_status to be either 'fully_tuned' or 'partially_tuned' for the rule_based_detection_accuracy countermeasure to activate. Additionally, this attribute feeds into the behavioral_baseline_deviation_detection rule. Untuned default rules generate excessive false positives and miss environment-specific threat patterns. Out-of-the-box vendor rules are designed for generic environments and will produce noise volumes that render the SIEM operationally unmanageable in most real-world deployments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SIEM administrator and security engineering team. Ask specifically whether rules use vendor default thresholds, whether environment-specific IP ranges and service accounts have been added to exclusion lists, and whether threshold values have been adjusted based on observed traffic volumes. Request evidence such as a list of modified rules vs. total rules.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented evidence of at least some rules having been modified from vendor defaults, with suppression lists or threshold configurations visible in the SIEM.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open the SIEM rule management interface and inspect a sample of 10–15 active correlation rules. Check for the presence of allowlist entries, exception conditions, customized threshold values, or environment-specific IP ranges. Compare against the vendor's published default rule configuration to identify customizations.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Content Management > Correlation Searches > select a rule > Review 'Adaptive Thresholds' and 'Notable Event Suppression' settings | QRadar: Rules > select rule > Building Blocks for local asset references | Sentinel: Analytics Rules > Edit rule > Entity mapping and suppression settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rule configurations showing custom threshold values, populated allowlists, or environment-specific conditions indicating tuning has occurred.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API to retrieve rule configurations and compare threshold and exception fields against vendor-published defaults. A high percentage of rules with non-default exception fields indicates tuning.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/rules?fields=name,thresholds,exceptions,allowlist' | jq '[.rules[] | select(.exceptions | length > 0)] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Count of rules with non-empty exception or allowlist fields; zero count indicates untuned_default status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM rule export files or version-controlled rule configurations. Compare current rule files against original vendor-provided baseline files to identify customizations. Rule files with unchanged thresholds, empty allowlists, and no local exception entries indicate untuned_default status.
how_to_obtain.command: diff <(cat /opt/siem/rules/vendor_defaults/*.yaml) <(cat /opt/siem/rules/production/*.yaml) | grep -E '^[<>].*threshold|allowlist|exclude'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Diff output showing lines modified from defaults in threshold or allowlist fields; no diff indicates untuned_default.

option_description: Measures the elapsed time in days since the SIEM correlation rule set was last formally reviewed and updated to address new threats, deprecated techniques, environmental changes such as new systems or decommissioned assets, and emerging attack vectors.
security_impact: The Rego policy for rule_based_detection_accuracy requires last_rule_review_days_ago <= 90. Rules that have not been reviewed within 90 days may reference decommissioned assets producing noise, miss newly identified threat techniques, contain stale IOCs, or fail to account for legitimate infrastructure changes that inflate false positives. A 90-day maximum review cycle aligns with quarterly threat landscape updates and standard change management cadences.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM change management interface or rule version history. Most enterprise SIEMs maintain an audit log showing the last-modified timestamp per rule. Identify the most recent rule set-level review event (not individual rule edits) and calculate days elapsed from that date to today.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Content Management > Correlation Searches > 'Last Modified' column, sort descending | Sentinel: Analytics > Rules > 'Last modified' column | QRadar: Rules > right-click > View Audit Log | Elastic: Security > Rules > Last updated column
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A date stamp indicating the last modification or formal review date for the active rule set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Calculate the days elapsed since the most recently modified rule file in the SIEM rules directory or version control repository.
how_to_obtain.command: find /opt/siem/rules/production -name '*.yaml' -o -name '*.json' | xargs ls -lt | head -1 | awk '{print $6, $7, $8}' | xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d "{}" +%s)) / 86400 )) days since last rule update'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A number of days elapsed, ideally 90 or fewer, since the most recent rule modification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM management API for the most recently modified rule and extract its last_updated timestamp. Calculate current date minus that timestamp in days.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/rules?sort=last_updated&order=desc&limit=1' | jq '(.rules[0].last_updated | fromdateiso8601) as $t | ((now - $t) / 86400) | floor'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing days elapsed since the last rule update; values greater than 90 indicate a stale rule set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the most recent SIEM rule review ticket or change record from the change management system (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira). The ticket close date represents the last formal review. If no tickets exist, rule review is not being formally tracked, which should itself be escalated as a finding.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A change management ticket or documented review record with a close date within the past 90 days.

option_description: Indicates whether the SIEM or integrated UEBA platform is actively running statistical baseline computation jobs for users, hosts, or other entities, establishing normal behavioral profiles against which anomalies can be detected.
security_impact: This is a prerequisite gate for the behavioral_baseline_deviation_detection Rego countermeasure. If baseline_modeling_enabled is false, the entire behavioral analytics capability fails regardless of how many deviation rules are configured, since those rules have no computed baselines to compare against. Behavioral baseline modeling is essential for detecting low-and-slow attacks, insider threats, and novel techniques that signature-based rules cannot identify.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the UEBA or behavioral analytics configuration section of the SIEM. Check for active machine learning or statistical baseline computation jobs. Verify that baseline computation is not disabled, paused, or in a degraded state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk UBA: Configuration > Data Sources > ML Models status | Microsoft Sentinel: UEBA Settings > Entity behavior analytics > Enable | Exabeam: Settings > Data Insights > Baseline status | QRadar UEBA: User Behavior Analytics > Configuration > Model Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Baseline modeling shows 'Active', 'Running', or 'Enabled' state with a recent last-computed timestamp.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the UEBA or SIEM analytics API to check the status of baseline modeling jobs or ML model computation pipelines.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/ueba/baseline_models' | jq '{enabled: .baseline_computation_enabled, last_run: .last_computed, model_count: (.models | length)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response showing baseline_computation_enabled as true with a recent last_computed timestamp.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk UBA or similar on-premises deployments, check the status of baseline computation daemons or scheduled jobs via the system service manager.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl status splunk-uba-baseline-engine 2>/dev/null || kubectl get pods -n siem-analytics -l component=baseline-engine --field-selector=status.phase=Running
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service or pod in 'active (running)' or 'Running' state indicating baseline computation is operational.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM or UEBA application logs for evidence of baseline computation job completions. Scheduled baseline jobs should produce completion log entries at defined intervals (typically daily or weekly). Absence of recent completion entries indicates baseline modeling is not running.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'baseline_computed\|model_trained\|profile_updated\|ueba.*complete' /var/log/siem/analytics.log | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing successful baseline computation completions within the past 24–48 hours.

option_description: Counts the total number of active SIEM or UEBA correlation rules and analytic models specifically configured to fire alerts when entity behavior deviates from their established statistical baselines, covering anomalies such as unusual login times, abnormal data volumes, or atypical access patterns.
security_impact: The Rego policy for behavioral_baseline_deviation_detection requires deviation_detection_rules_count >= 1, meaning at least one active behavioral deviation rule must exist for the countermeasure to register. Higher counts provide broader behavioral coverage. Environments with zero active deviation rules have no capability to detect insider threats, account compromise via stolen credentials, or low-and-slow exfiltration that does not match known signatures.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SIEM or UEBA rule management interface. Filter the active rules list by category tags such as 'behavioral', 'anomaly', 'UEBA', 'deviation', or 'ML'. Count the total number of rules returned that are in an enabled or active state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Content Management > Correlation Searches > filter tag='anomaly' AND status='active' | Sentinel: Analytics > filter Rule type='Anomaly' or 'ML Behavior Analytics' > count enabled | Exabeam: Rules > Filter by Type=Behavioral > count active | QRadar: Rules > filter by 'anomaly' building block
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of rules in the behavioral or anomaly category with active/enabled status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API for rules tagged with behavioral or anomaly categories in enabled state and return the total count.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/rules?category=behavioral&status=enabled' | jq '.total_count // (.rules | length)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of enabled behavioral/anomaly detection rules; any value >= 1 satisfies the minimum Rego threshold.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk ES, query the saved searches endpoint and filter for correlation searches with anomaly or behavioral tags in enabled state.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches?search=tags%3Danomalous+OR+tags%3Dbehavioral&output_mode=json' | jq '[.entry[] | select(.content.disabled==false)] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of non-disabled anomaly or behavioral correlation searches.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request a rule inventory report from the SIEM administrator that includes rule type classification. Ask specifically how many rules rely on UEBA scores, risk scoring, or behavioral baseline comparisons rather than static threshold matching. If no classification exists, this indicates poor rule governance.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented count of behavioral detection rules, ideally broken out from static signature rules, demonstrating deliberate coverage planning.

option_description: Defines the breadth of entity types for which active behavioral baseline profiles exist within the SIEM or UEBA platform. 'Full' coverage includes all critical entity types such as users, privileged accounts, hosts, service accounts, and applications. 'Partial' means only a subset of entity types are profiled. 'None' means no baseline profiles have been computed.
security_impact: The Rego policy for behavioral_baseline_deviation_detection requires baseline_coverage_scope to be either 'partial' or 'full'. A scope of 'none' disqualifies the behavioral detection countermeasure entirely. Limited scope creates detection blind spots: an environment that baselines only users but not service accounts or hosts will miss lateral movement, service account abuse, and host-based anomalies that are hallmarks of advanced persistent threats and ransomware precursor activity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the UEBA or entity analytics configuration section and review which entity types have active baseline profile categories. Check for dedicated profile tabs or sections for Users, Hosts, Service Accounts, Applications, and Cloud Resources. Confirm each category shows a non-zero entity count with recent baseline update timestamps.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk UBA: Configuration > Entity Types > check Users, Hosts, Machines with active model counts | Sentinel: Entity Behavior > Settings > confirm entity types monitored | Exabeam: User Intelligence > Settings > Peer Groups and entity types | QRadar UEBA: User Behavior Analytics > Monitored Entity Types
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All critical entity type categories (users, hosts, service accounts) show active profiles with recent computation dates indicating 'full' scope; subset indicates 'partial'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the UEBA API for the list of entity types with active baseline profiles and confirm which categories are populated.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/ueba/entities/profile_summary' | jq '{entity_types_with_baselines: [.entity_types[] | select(.baseline_count > 0) | .type], total_entity_types: (.entity_types | length)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON listing entity types with active baselines; presence of users, hosts, and service_accounts indicates 'full' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the UEBA or SIEM analytics owner to enumerate which entity categories are actively profiled. Request a written inventory showing entity type, number of profiled entities, and date of most recent baseline computation. Ask whether service accounts and non-human identities are included, as these are commonly missed.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented entity type coverage list. If users only are covered, classify as 'partial'. If users, hosts, service accounts, and applications are covered, classify as 'full'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the UEBA platform's baseline computation logs to identify which entity type categories have had recent baseline updates. Entity types with no log entries for baseline computation in the past 30 days should be treated as uncovered.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'baseline_computed|profile_built|entity_type' /var/log/ueba/model-engine.log | grep -v 'ERROR\|WARN' | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries listing entity_type values with computation counts; presence of user, host, service_account entries indicates breadth of coverage.

option_description: Enumerates the distinct categories of log sources actively connected to and ingesting data into the SIEM, such as endpoint, network, application, cloud, identity, email, and OT/ICS. This array reflects the breadth of visibility available for correlation rule matching.
security_impact: The Rego policy for multi_source_log_correlation requires count(log_source_types_integrated) >= 3 when combined with cross-source correlation rules to activate the countermeasure, or >= 2 sources with five or more active cross-source rules for an alternate path. Each missing source category creates a detection blind spot: without network logs, lateral movement goes unseen; without identity logs, credential abuse is undetectable; without cloud logs, cloud-native attacks are invisible. The array content also directly determines which correlation rules can function meaningfully.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SIEM data source or connector management console and review the list of configured and actively ingesting data source connectors. Document each unique category represented (e.g., if multiple EDR products are connected, count as one 'endpoint' category). Verify each connector shows a recent last-received timestamp within the past hour to confirm active ingestion.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Data Inputs > monitor active forwarders by sourcetype | Sentinel: Data Connectors > filter by 'Connected' status | QRadar: Admin > Log Sources > filter by 'Active' status | Elastic: Stack Management > Beats > active shippers by type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of connected data source categories each showing active/connected status with recent last-event timestamps, enumerable into a distinct category array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM data source management API to retrieve the list of active log source connectors and extract distinct source type categories.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/data_sources?status=active' | jq '[.sources[].category] | unique | sort'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON array of unique source category strings such as ["cloud", "endpoint", "identity", "network"]; length >= 3 satisfies the primary Rego threshold.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk deployments, query the internal search index to enumerate distinct sourcetypes receiving data in the past 24 hours, then manually map sourcetypes to source categories.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS -X POST 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' --data 'search=index=* earliest=-24h | stats latest(_time) as last_seen by index, sourcetype | where last_seen > relative_time(now(), "-1h") | stats values(sourcetype) by index&output_mode=json' | jq '[.results[].sourcetype] | unique'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of unique sourcetypes with recent data; analyst maps these to source categories (e.g., WinEventLog=endpoint, cisco:asa=network, o365:azure:aad=identity).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM's data source configuration manifest or deployment inventory file to enumerate configured log collectors and their assigned source type categories. This provides a configuration-level view which should be cross-referenced against actual ingestion status.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /opt/siem/config/data_sources.yaml | grep -E 'category:|type:|enabled:' | paste - - - | awk '/enabled: true/{print $2}' | sort | uniq
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of enabled source categories from the configuration file; should be validated against live ingestion data to confirm categories are actively forwarding logs.

option_description: Controls whether the SIEM has at least one active correlation rule that joins events from two or more distinct log source categories (e.g., endpoint + network, identity + cloud) to construct multi-stage attack chains that no single source would surface independently.
security_impact: Directly gates the multi_source_log_correlation countermeasure in the Rego policy. The policy requires cross_source_correlation_rules_enabled == true alongside active_cross_source_rule_count >= 1 and alert_output_configured == true for the 3-source path. Without this, correlated attack chain detection is entirely absent, leaving lateral movement, credential theft followed by data exfiltration, and similar multi-hop campaigns undetectable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM rule management console (e.g., Splunk ES > Security Content > Correlation Rules, Microsoft Sentinel > Analytics, or IBM QRadar > Rules). Filter rules by status 'Active/Enabled' and inspect the data source field or log type mappings for each rule. Confirm at least one rule references two or more distinct source categories such as Windows Event Logs AND network flow data.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Analytics/Correlation Rules > Filter: Status=Enabled > Inspect Data Sources column
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one enabled rule showing multiple source type references (e.g., 'endpoint' AND 'network' or 'identity' AND 'cloud audit')

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Splunk Enterprise Security, query the correlation search knowledge object store to find searches referencing multiple index or sourcetype values.
how_to_obtain.command: | rest /servicesNS/-/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches splunk_server=local | where like('action.correlationsearch.enabled', '1') | eval sources=mvcount(split('dispatch.index', ',')) | where sources > 1 | table title, dispatch.index, action.correlationsearch.enabled
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more rows returned indicating active correlation searches spanning multiple indexes/sourcetypes

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM REST API to retrieve active correlation rules and inspect their source type bindings. Example for Microsoft Sentinel using Azure REST API.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/{workspace}/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/alertRules?api-version=2023-02-01' -H 'Authorization: Bearer {token}' | jq '[.value[] | select(.properties.enabled==true) | select(.properties.queryFrequency != null)] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing enabled analytic rules; manually inspect query text for multi-table joins (e.g., SecurityEvent JOIN AzureActivity)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM audit or configuration export logs for rule definitions. In QRadar, export the rule list from the Rules page and check the 'Log Source Type' filter columns for rules marked Active.
how_to_obtain.navigation: QRadar Console > Offenses > Rules > Export to CSV > Filter column 'Log Source Group' for multi-value entries
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exported CSV shows at least one active rule with multiple distinct log source group values

option_description: Represents the total count of currently enabled SIEM correlation rules that reference and join events from two or more distinct log source type categories. This integer provides a quantitative measure of cross-source detection breadth.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this value in two paths for multi_source_log_correlation: the primary path requires active_cross_source_rule_count >= 1 when three or more source types are integrated and cross_source_correlation_rules_enabled is true; the secondary path requires active_cross_source_rule_count >= 5 even with only two integrated source types. A count of zero completely prevents this countermeasure from activating. Higher counts indicate broader coverage of multi-stage attack scenarios.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk Enterprise Security, count correlation searches that join across multiple sourcetypes or indexes using the REST endpoint.
how_to_obtain.command: | rest /servicesNS/-/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches splunk_server=local count=0 | where like('action.correlationsearch.enabled','1') AND (like(search, '%join%') OR like(search, '%union%') OR match(search, 'index=\w+ .* index=\w+')) | stats count as active_cross_source_rule_count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A single integer value reflecting the count of active multi-source correlation searches

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Microsoft Sentinel REST API to retrieve all enabled scheduled query rules, then parse query text for multi-table or multi-workspace joins and count results.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/{ws}/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/alertRules?api-version=2023-02-01' -H 'Authorization: Bearer {token}' | jq '[.value[] | select(.properties.enabled==true) | select(.properties.query | test("join|union"; "i"))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of enabled rules with multi-source joins in their query logic

how_to_obtain.instruction: In IBM QRadar, navigate to the Rules center and filter by 'Type = Event' and 'Status = Active'. Use column grouping or export to count rules whose 'Log Source Type(s)' field contains more than one distinct source category.
how_to_obtain.navigation: QRadar > Offenses > Rules > Filter (Type=Event, Status=Active) > Export > Count rows with multiple Log Source Types
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Numeric count of exported rule rows where the Log Source Type column lists two or more distinct categories

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SIEM engineering or SOC engineering team and request the current rule inventory report. Ask specifically for a breakdown of rules by number of log source types referenced. Many organizations maintain this in a spreadsheet or CMDB linked to the SIEM.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented count of active multi-source rules, ideally from a rule management register or SIEM platform report

option_description: Controls whether correlation rule matches are wired to produce actionable downstream output—such as SIEM alerts visible in analyst queues, incident tickets in ITSM platforms, or SOAR playbook triggers—ensuring rule matches translate into analyst-visible or automated response actions rather than silently firing.
security_impact: Required by the Rego policy in both evaluation paths for multi_source_log_correlation. Even with cross-source rules enabled and sufficient rule counts, if alert_output_configured is false or null, the countermeasure does not activate. Rules that fire without output actions represent detection capability that is operationally invisible, providing zero security value since no analyst or automation acts on the detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open each active correlation rule in the SIEM rule editor and inspect the 'Actions' or 'Response Actions' tab. Verify that at least one action is configured (e.g., 'Create Notable Event', 'Send Email', 'Trigger Webhook', 'Create SOAR case'). In Splunk ES, check that 'notable' action is enabled on correlation searches.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES > Content Management > Correlation Searches > Edit Rule > Alert Actions tab > Verify 'notable' or other action is checked
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one action type enabled per rule—'Create Notable Event', 'Send to SOAR', or equivalent webhook/ticket action visible

option_description: Controls whether the SIEM platform is configured to assign explicit, structured severity classifications (e.g., Critical/High/Medium/Low or a numeric score) to generated alerts based on defined logic within correlation rules, rather than leaving severity as a default or unset value.
security_impact: Serves as a prerequisite boolean gate in both Rego policy paths for alert_triage_and_prioritization. If severity_scoring_enabled is false, neither the high-fidelity path (requiring multi_tier severity and 80% coverage) nor the baseline path (requiring binary/multi_tier and 60% coverage) can activate this countermeasure. Without severity scoring, analysts cannot distinguish critical incidents from low-priority noise, degrading mean time to respond (MTTR) for high-impact events.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM alert or rule configuration interface, open several active correlation rules and inspect whether a 'Severity' or 'Priority' field is set to an explicit non-default value. In Splunk ES, check the Notable Event Settings within correlation searches for the 'Severity' dropdown. In Sentinel, check the 'Alert severity' field in analytic rule settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES > Content Management > Correlation Searches > Edit > Notable Event Settings > Severity field; OR Sentinel > Analytics > Edit Rule > Set rule logic > Alert severity dropdown
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Severity field shows an explicit value (e.g., 'High', 'Critical', '7') rather than 'default', 'inherited', or blank

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, query the correlation search definitions to check whether severity is explicitly set versus relying on defaults.
how_to_obtain.command: | rest /servicesNS/-/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches splunk_server=local count=0 | where like('action.correlationsearch.enabled','1') | eval has_severity=if(isnotnull('action.notable.param.severity') AND 'action.notable.param.severity'!="", "yes", "no") | stats count by has_severity
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Majority of rules showing has_severity='yes'; if any show 'no', severity scoring is partially or not enabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Sentinel alert rules API to check whether the alertSeverity property is explicitly set on enabled rules.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/{ws}/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/alertRules?api-version=2023-02-01' -H 'Authorization: Bearer {token}' | jq '[.value[] | select(.properties.enabled==true) | {name: .properties.displayName, severity: .properties.severity}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each enabled rule returns a non-null severity value (High, Medium, Low, or Informational); absence indicates scoring not configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Pull a sample of recent SIEM alerts from the alert index or incident table and check whether the severity field is populated with meaningful values. In Splunk, search the notable events index.
how_to_obtain.command: index=notable earliest=-7d | stats count by severity | sort -count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Results showing distinct severity levels (e.g., critical, high, medium, low) with non-zero counts; single value or all 'unknown' indicates scoring is not properly enabled

option_description: Controls whether an analyst-facing workflow—such as a SIEM queue sorted by severity, a dashboard view that surfaces highest-severity alerts first, or a ticketing/case management integration that respects severity ordering—is actively configured to direct analyst attention to the most critical alerts before lower-priority ones.
security_impact: Required alongside severity_scoring_enabled in both Rego policy paths for alert_triage_and_prioritization. Even with perfect severity scoring, if no workflow enforces priority ordering, analysts may process alerts in arrival order (FIFO), causing critical incidents to be delayed behind medium or low alerts. This directly degrades MTTD and MTTR for high-severity events and prevents the countermeasure from activating in the policy evaluation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM analyst dashboard or incident queue, verify that alerts are sorted by severity descending by default. In Splunk ES, check the Incident Review dashboard sort configuration. In ServiceNow SIEM integration, confirm that P1 incidents appear at the top of the security incident queue. Confirm the sort order persists for new analyst sessions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES > Incident Review > Verify default sort = 'Urgency (Highest First)'; OR SOAR > Queues > Verify severity-based routing rules; OR ServiceNow > Security Incident Response > Queue view > Sort by Priority
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert queue or dashboard displays highest severity alerts at the top by default without manual analyst intervention

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM dashboard or triage queue configuration file to confirm sort order and severity filter settings are explicitly defined. In Splunk, review the Incident Review savedsearch configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration stanza for Incident Review shows 'sort' parameter referencing urgency or severity in descending order

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SOAR platform API to confirm playbook routing rules that assign tickets to queues or analysts based on alert severity are active and bound to detection rules.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://{soar-host}/rest/playbook?_filter_active=true&_filter_name__icontains=triage' -H 'ph-auth-token: {token}' | jq '[.data[] | select(.active==true) | {name: .name, trigger: .trigger}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active playbooks returned with trigger conditions referencing severity or priority fields, indicating workflow automation is configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview SOC analysts and team leads to confirm whether there is a documented or enforced process requiring analysts to work their alert queue from highest to lowest severity. Request screenshots or recordings of the analyst interface showing the default queue sort order.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Analyst confirms queue is sorted by severity by default and provides screen evidence; documented SOP references severity-first triage process

option_description: Represents the granularity of severity classification tiers formally defined within the SIEM's correlation rule schema. 'none' means no severity tiers are defined; 'binary' means two tiers (e.g., high/low or alert/no-alert); 'multi_tier' means three or more distinct levels (e.g., Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational) are defined and applied.
security_impact: Used as a discriminating factor between two Rego policy paths for alert_triage_and_prioritization. The high-fidelity path requires severity_levels_defined == 'multi_tier' AND coverage >= 80%. The baseline path accepts 'binary' or 'multi_tier' but requires only >= 60% coverage. A value of 'none' prevents both paths from activating. Multi-tier severity enables finer-grained analyst prioritization and more precise escalation thresholds than binary classification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM alert or rule configuration and inspect the available values in the 'Severity' or 'Priority' dropdown field within rule definitions. Count the number of distinct selectable options. In Splunk ES, check the severity lookup table. In Microsoft Sentinel, observe the Alert severity options when editing an analytic rule.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES > Configuration > Data Enrichment > Lists and Lookups > urgency_lookup; OR Sentinel > Analytics > Edit Rule > Alert severity dropdown (options: High/Medium/Low/Informational = multi_tier)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 4+ severity options are visible (e.g., Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational), classify as 'multi_tier'; 2 options = 'binary'; no options or field absent = 'none'

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, inspect the urgency or severity lookup table to enumerate the defined severity tiers.
how_to_obtain.command: | inputlookup urgency_lookup | stats dc(urgency) as tier_count, values(urgency) as tiers | eval classification=case(tier_count==0, "none", tier_count==1 OR tier_count==2, "binary", tier_count>=3, "multi_tier")
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows tier_count >= 3 and classification = 'multi_tier' for a well-configured environment; tiers list shows Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational or equivalent

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM severity taxonomy configuration file or rule schema definition. In Splunk, examine the urgency or severity field definitions in the ES configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'severity\|urgency\|priority' /opt/splunk/etc/apps/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/default/transforms.conf | grep -A5 'urgency'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration file shows explicit enumeration of severity values; count distinct values to classify as none/binary/multi_tier

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the alert severity schema from the SIEM or SOAR API to enumerate valid severity classifications and count distinct tiers.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://{soar-host}/rest/severity' -H 'ph-auth-token: {token}' | jq '[.data[] | .name] | length, .'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API response listing severity objects; count >= 3 indicates multi_tier, count == 2 indicates binary, count == 0 or absent indicates none

option_description: Represents the percentage of all currently active SIEM correlation rules that have an explicit, non-default severity value assigned. Calculated as (count of rules with explicit severity / total active rules) × 100. Rules relying on platform default or having no severity value do not count toward this percentage.
security_impact: Used as a threshold condition in both Rego policy paths for alert_triage_and_prioritization. The high-fidelity path requires coverage >= 80% (combined with multi_tier severity), while the baseline path requires >= 60% (with binary or multi_tier). Below 60%, neither path activates even if severity scoring is enabled globally. A low percentage means a significant fraction of rule matches generate alerts with no meaningful priority signal, creating analyst blind spots for those detections.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, calculate the percentage of active correlation searches that have an explicit severity assignment versus total active correlation searches.
how_to_obtain.command: | rest /servicesNS/-/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches splunk_server=local count=0 | where like('action.correlationsearch.enabled','1') | eval has_severity=if(isnotnull('action.notable.param.severity') AND 'action.notable.param.severity'!="" AND 'action.notable.param.severity'!="default", 1, 0) | stats sum(has_severity) as with_severity, count as total | eval coverage_pct=round((with_severity/total)*100, 0) | table with_severity, total, coverage_pct
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Single row showing with_severity count, total count, and coverage_pct as an integer between 0 and 100; target >= 80 for high-fidelity compliance

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Microsoft Sentinel REST API to retrieve all enabled analytic rules and calculate what percentage have an explicit (non-null) severity value set.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/{ws}/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/alertRules?api-version=2023-02-01' -H 'Authorization: Bearer {token}' | jq '([ .value[] | select(.properties.enabled==true) ] | length) as $total | ([ .value[] | select(.properties.enabled==true) | select(.properties.severity != null and .properties.severity != "") ] | length) as $with_sev | {total: $total, with_severity: $with_sev, coverage_pct: (($with_sev / $total) * 100 | round)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object with total, with_severity, and coverage_pct fields; coverage_pct >= 80 satisfies the high-fidelity policy path

how_to_obtain.instruction: Export the full active rule list from the SIEM rule management interface. Open in a spreadsheet application and create a formula to count rows where the Severity/Priority column is populated with a specific non-default value, then divide by total rule count and multiply by 100.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Rule Management > Export All Active Rules (CSV/Excel) > Spreadsheet: =COUNTIF(SeverityCol,"<>"&"")/COUNTA(SeverityCol)*100
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Calculated percentage between 0 and 100; values < 60 indicate a compliance gap, 60-79 meets baseline policy path, >= 80 meets high-fidelity path

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the SIEM team's rule inventory or health report, which in mature organizations is generated weekly or monthly. Ask for a breakdown showing how many active rules have explicit severity versus default or unset severity.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented percentage from a rule inventory report; acceptable evidence for audit purposes if generated within the last 30 days

option_description: Controls whether the SIEM or integrated SOAR platform has at least one automated response action—such as account lockout, firewall rule push, host isolation, or incident ticket creation—configured, active, and bound to a triggered detection rule so that it executes without requiring manual analyst intervention.
security_impact: Serves as the primary boolean gate for the automated_response_orchestration countermeasure in the Rego policy. The policy requires automated_response_actions_enabled == true combined with rules_with_response_coverage_pct >= 50 and at least one defined response_action_type. If false, this countermeasure cannot activate regardless of SOAR platform availability. Automated response directly reduces dwell time by enabling machine-speed containment actions for known threat patterns without waiting for analyst availability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SOAR platform or SIEM response action configuration. In Splunk SOAR, check the Playbooks section for active playbooks with automation enabled. In Microsoft Sentinel, check Analytics rules for configured automation rules under 'Automation'. In Palo Alto XSOAR, verify active playbooks are triggered by alert type. Confirm at least one playbook has 'active' status and is bound to a detection source.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Sentinel > Automation > Automation Rules > Verify status=Active with 'Run playbook' action; OR Splunk SOAR > Playbooks > Filter Active=True > Confirm trigger type matches alert source; OR QRadar > Admin > Automated Responses > Verify at least one rule has an active response action
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one automation rule or playbook is shown as Active and configured to trigger on alert/detection rule match with a specific response action (lockout, block, isolate, or ticket creation)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Splunk SOAR REST API to check for active playbooks that contain automated response actions.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -k -X GET 'https://{soar-host}/rest/playbook?_filter_active=true&page_size=50' -H 'ph-auth-token: {token}' | jq '{total_active: .count, playbooks: [.data[] | {name: .name, active: .active, automated: .is_default}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response shows total_active > 0 with at least one playbook marked active; review playbook details to confirm automated actions (not just manual) are configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Sentinel Automation Rules API to verify that active automation rules with playbook execution actions exist.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{subId}/resourceGroups/{rg}/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/{ws}/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/automationRules?api-version=2023-02-01' -H 'Authorization: Bearer {token}' | jq '[.value[] | select(.properties.triggeringLogic.isEnabled==true) | select(.properties.actions[].actionType=="RunPlaybook")] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer > 0 indicating enabled automation rules that trigger playbook execution; 0 means automated response is not configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SOAR or SIEM response action configuration files to verify that response action definitions are present and enabled. In QRadar, inspect the Custom Actions configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'response_action\|automated_action\|playbook_trigger' /opt/qradar/conf/ --include='*.conf' | grep -i 'enabled\|active'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries showing enabled=true or active=1 for at least one automated response action definition bound to a correlation rule

option_description: Enumerates the distinct categories of automated response actions configured and bound to detection rules in the SIEM/SOAR platform, such as account_lockout, firewall_block, ticket_creation, and endpoint_isolation. This inventory defines the breadth of the automated response arsenal available for threat containment.
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_response_orchestration requires count(input.response_action_types) >= 1 to activate the countermeasure. A richer set of action types (e.g., account lockout, firewall block, endpoint isolation) reduces dwell time by enabling proportional, automated containment without manual analyst intervention. An empty or minimal list means detections produce alerts only, leaving containment entirely dependent on human response speed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk SOAR, navigate to Apps > Apps & Assets and review configured playbook action categories. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to Automation > Playbooks and enumerate the action types in each active Logic App. In Palo Alto XSOAR, navigate to Automation > Playbooks and inspect the action block types used.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk SOAR: Apps > Apps & Assets | Sentinel: Automation > Playbooks | XSOAR: Automation > Playbooks
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of action categories such as 'account_lockout', 'firewall_block', 'ticket_creation', 'endpoint_isolation', 'email_notification'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Splunk SOAR REST API to retrieve all configured action types across active playbooks.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<password> https://<soar-host>/rest/action_run?page_size=0 | jq '[.data[].action] | unique'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON array of unique action type strings representing all action categories bound to playbooks, e.g. ["block ip", "disable user", "create ticket"]

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Sentinel automation rules via Azure REST API to enumerate all action types configured in active automation rules and playbooks.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method get --url 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/<ws>/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/automationRules?api-version=2023-02-01' | jq '[.value[].properties.actions[].actionType] | unique'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC engineering team and request the current SOAR playbook inventory document. Ask for a mapping of each playbook to its primary action category and cross-reference against the SIEM detection rule triggers to confirm each action type is actively bound to at least one rule.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented list of response action categories with confirmation that each is mapped to at least one active detection rule

option_description: Measures the percentage of currently active SIEM/SOAR detection rules that have at least one automated response action bound to them. This metric quantifies how much of the detection estate is backed by automated containment versus alert-only logic.
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_response_orchestration requires input.rules_with_response_coverage_pct >= 50 to satisfy the countermeasure condition. Values below 50% indicate that the majority of detections rely on manual analyst response, significantly increasing mean time to contain (MTTC). A higher percentage demonstrates that detections are paired with actionable, automated containment, directly reducing dwell time for matched threats.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, query the correlation search configuration to count total enabled rules and those with an alert action configured that triggers a SOAR playbook or adaptive response action.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<password> https://<splunk-host>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/saved/searches?search=action.correlationsearch.enabled%3D1&count=0&output_mode=json | jq '{total: .paging.total, with_response: [.entry[] | select(.content."action.notable.param.drilldown_search" != null or .content."actions" | test("notable|risk|logevent"))] | length}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON object showing total active rules and count with response actions, from which percentage can be calculated as (with_response / total) * 100

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Sentinel, use the Azure REST API to retrieve all enabled analytics rules and check which ones have associated automation rules or playbook triggers.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method get --url 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/<ws>/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/alertRules?api-version=2023-02-01' | jq '{total: (.value | length), enabled: [.value[] | select(.properties.enabled == true)] | length}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Counts of total and enabled rules; cross-reference with automation rule triggers to determine which have response actions, then calculate percentage

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, navigate to Configure > Content Management, filter by type 'Correlation Search', and export the list. Filter for enabled searches and those with 'Adaptive Response Actions' or 'Notable Event' actions configured. In Sentinel, go to Analytics > Active Rules and filter for rules with Automation attached.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Configure > Content Management > Correlation Searches | Sentinel: Analytics > Active Rules > filter by Automation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exportable list of rules; calculate (rules with response / total active rules) * 100 to arrive at the percentage

how_to_obtain.instruction: For QRadar, use the REST API to list all enabled custom rules and those with response actions (e.g., email, offense routing to SOAR).
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'SEC: <api_token>' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<qradar-host>/api/analytics/rules?fields=id,name,enabled,response_limiters&filter=enabled%3Dtrue' | jq '{total: length, with_response: [.[] | select(.response_limiters | length > 0)] | length}'

option_description: The total count of currently enabled and active SIEM correlation and detection rules across the platform. This represents the breadth of the detection engine — every enabled rule contributes to identifying specific threat behaviors or anomalies in ingested log data.

A low rule count creates significant detection blind spots. This metric is a primary indicator of detection posture maturity — environments with fewer than 50 rules are critically underserved and unable to achieve the coverage breadth countermeasure.

how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the total count of enabled rules in QRadar, e.g. 312

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, navigate to Configure > Content Management, set filter to 'Correlation Search' and Status 'Enabled', and observe the total count displayed in the results summary. In Sentinel, go to Analytics > Active Rules and note the total number shown.
