option_description: A boolean indicator confirming whether the complete set of active detection rules has been formally reviewed and validated within the past 90 days. This review process verifies that rules are current, accurately tuned to the environment, and not generating excessive false positives or covering deprecated threat scenarios.
security_impact: The Rego policy's primary path for detection_rule_coverage_breadth requires input.rules_reviewed_within_90_days == true alongside adequate rule count and MITRE coverage. Without recent review, stale rules may fire on obsolete log formats, miss new attack techniques, or generate excessive false positives that cause alert fatigue. The 90-day threshold aligns with the rule_tuning_and_operational_maintainability countermeasure's review cycle requirement, ensuring detection logic remains operationally relevant.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the SIEM platform audit logs for entries indicating a bulk rule review activity — look for mass rule enable/disable events, version updates, or comments/annotations added within the past 90 days.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(rule_review|correlation_search.*modified|analytics_rule.*updated)' /var/log/siem-audit.log | awk -F'|' '$1 > date -d "-90 days" +%Y%m%d {print}' 2>/dev/null || journalctl -u splunkd --since '90 days ago' | grep -i 'savedsearch.*update'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries dated within the last 90 days showing rule review or modification activity by detection engineering team members

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request evidence from the detection engineering or SOC management team: look for change management tickets (ServiceNow, Jira) tagged with 'rule review', 'detection review', or 'SIEM tuning' closed within the past 90 days. Check for meeting minutes or review reports from a formal rule review session.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A change ticket, review report, or documented meeting outcome dated within the last 90 days confirming systematic rule review was completed

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Sentinel, query the audit log for analytics rule modification events within the last 90 days to confirm a systematic review occurred.
how_to_obtain.command: az monitor activity-log list --start-time $(date -d '-90 days' +%Y-%m-%d) --query "[?contains(operationName.value, 'alertRules')].{date:eventTimestamp, op:operationName.value, user:caller}" --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of analytics rule modification events within 90 days; a systematic review would show multiple rules updated by a security team member in a condensed timeframe

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review version control repository (Git) for detection rules if the team uses a GitOps/Detection-as-Code workflow. Check the git log for commits within the past 90 days touching rule files.
how_to_obtain.command: git -C /path/to/detection-rules log --since='90 days ago' --oneline --name-only | grep -E '\.(yml|yaml|json|spl)$' | sort -u | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of rule files modified in the past 90 days; a comprehensive review would show a large proportion of the rule inventory modified in a single sprint or review cycle

typical_values: false (no formal review process or review overdue)
true (review completed within 90-day window with documented evidence)

option_description: A boolean indicator confirming whether all critical log source categories — including network perimeter devices (firewalls, proxies), identity infrastructure (Active Directory, LDAP, SSO), endpoint agents (EDR/AV), and cloud service logs (AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity, GCP Audit) — are fully configured and actively sending logs to the SIEM. This represents the foundational data coverage prerequisite for effective detection.
security_impact: The Rego policy for log_ingestion_completeness requires input.critical_sources_onboarded == true as a mandatory condition — the countermeasure cannot be satisfied without it. Missing critical sources create absolute detection blind spots: an adversary operating exclusively through an unmonitored vector (e.g., cloud control plane, VPN concentrator) will generate no SIEM events regardless of how many rules are active. This is a foundational prerequisite for all detection capabilities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM platform, navigate to the data source management or health dashboard. In Splunk, go to Settings > Data Inputs or use the ES Data Source Monitoring dashboard. In Sentinel, go to Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Connectors. Compare the configured source list against the authoritative asset inventory for critical asset categories.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Security > Monitoring > Data Source Monitoring | Sentinel: Configuration > Data Connectors | QRadar: Admin > Log Sources
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of configured data connectors showing connection status; verify all critical categories (firewall, DC/AD, EDR, cloud) appear as 'Connected' or 'Receiving data'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Splunk for the list of distinct sourcetypes received in the past 24 hours and cross-reference against a required critical source list.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<password> -d 'search=| metadata type=sourcetypes index=* | search recentTime > relative_time(now(), "-24h") | table sourcetype,recentTime | sort -recentTime' -d 'output_mode=json' -d 'exec_mode=oneshot' 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' | jq '.results[].sourcetype'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of active sourcetypes; manually verify presence of critical categories: firewall (pan:traffic, cisco:asa), identity (WinEventLog:Security, msad), EDR (crowdstrike, carbonblack), cloud (aws:cloudtrail, azure:activity)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Sentinel data connectors API to list all connected data connectors and their status.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method get --url 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/<ws>/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/dataConnectors?api-version=2023-02-01' | jq '.value[] | {name: .name, kind: .kind, state: .properties.dataTypes}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of configured connectors with their types; verify critical categories are present and enabled: AzureActiveDirectory, MicrosoftDefenderAdvancedThreatProtection, AmazonWebServicesCloudTrail, CEF/Syslog for network devices

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the SIEM data source inventory document from the SOC team and compare it against the authoritative CMDB or asset inventory. Confirm that each critical asset category has a documented, approved log connector with a data owner and last-validated date.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A coverage matrix showing critical asset categories (perimeter, identity, endpoint, cloud, OT/IoT if applicable) each mapped to at least one active, validated log connector in the SIEM

typical_values: false (common in organizations with partial SIEM deployments or cloud blind spots)
true (all critical source categories validated and actively ingesting)

option_description: The percentage of all configured log sources that are actively and continuously streaming data to the SIEM within their expected heartbeat or polling interval. A source is considered healthy if it has delivered events within its defined SLA window (e.g., within 15 minutes for security tools, 1 hour for network devices). This metric quantifies the operational reliability of the data pipeline.
security_impact: The Rego policy for log_ingestion_completeness requires input.log_feed_health_percent >= 95, making this a high-threshold requirement. Even if all critical sources are onboarded, a feed health percentage below 95% means at minimum 1 in 20 sources is silently failing — creating unpredictable detection gaps that may not be immediately apparent. Degraded feeds are a common failure mode during incidents where adversaries target logging infrastructure specifically to blind detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SIEM data source health dashboard. In Splunk, use the 'Monitoring Console > Indexing > Indexing Performance' or install the 'Data Source Health' app. In Sentinel, check the 'Data Collection Health' workbook under Workbooks. In QRadar, navigate to Admin > System Monitoring > Log Source Management.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Monitoring Console > Indexing > Data Sources | Sentinel: Workbooks > Data Collection Health | QRadar: Admin > Log Source Management > Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dashboard showing each configured source with a health status indicator and last-event timestamp; calculate (healthy sources / total configured sources) * 100

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, query the internal index to identify sources that have not sent data within the expected interval and calculate the health percentage.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<password> -d 'search=| tstats count WHERE index=* earliest=-1h by host,source | stats count as active_sources | appendcols [| inputlookup asset_inventory.csv | stats count as total_sources] | eval health_pct=round((active_sources/total_sources)*100,1)' -d 'output_mode=json' -d 'exec_mode=oneshot' 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs/export'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A result showing active_sources, total_sources, and health_pct; target >= 95

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Sentinel Log Analytics workspace to identify data tables with no recent ingestion activity.
how_to_obtain.command: az monitor log-analytics query -w <workspace-id> --analytics-query 'union withsource=TableName * | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | summarize LastEvent=max(TimeGenerated) by TableName | where LastEvent < ago(30m) | project TableName, MinutesSinceLastEvent=datetime_diff("minute", now(), LastEvent)' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of data tables with stale ingestion; use total table count vs stale count to calculate health percentage; target: 0 or minimal stale sources

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the QRadar REST API to retrieve log source status and count sources with recent activity versus total configured sources.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'SEC: <api_token>' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<qradar-host>/api/config/event_sources/log_source_management/log_sources?fields=id,name,status,last_event_time&filter=enabled%3Dtrue' | jq '{total: length, healthy: [.[] | select(.last_event_time > ((now - 3600) * 1000))] | length} | .health_pct = (.healthy / .total * 100)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object with total sources, healthy sources, and calculated health_pct; target >= 95

typical_values: 70-80 (common in large enterprises with unmanaged log connector sprawl)
85-92 (typical managed SIEM deployments with some legacy source issues)
95-98 (target threshold per policy; mature SOC with active monitoring)
99-100 (advanced programs with automated feed health alerting and rapid remediation SLAs)

option_description: The absolute count of configured log sources that have exceeded their defined maximum silence threshold — meaning no events have been received within the expected ingestion window (e.g., >24 hours for network infrastructure, >1 hour for security tools like EDR or IDPS). Each silent source represents a specific, identifiable detection blind spot in the environment.
security_impact: The Rego policy for log_ingestion_completeness requires input.stale_or_silent_source_count == 0 — any non-zero value prevents the countermeasure from being satisfied. This is the strictest condition in the log_ingestion_completeness rule, requiring complete elimination of silent sources. A single silent domain controller or firewall can represent thousands of missed authentication events or network connections. Silent sources also commonly indicate that an adversary has disabled logging as part of defense evasion (MITRE ATT&CK T1562.001).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, search for configured hosts or sources in the asset inventory that have not appeared in index data within the defined silence threshold.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:<password> -d 'search=| inputlookup asset_inventory.csv | eval expected_host=host | join type=left expected_host [| tstats latest(_time) as last_seen WHERE index=* earliest=-48h by host] | eval hours_silent=round((now()-last_seen)/3600,1) | where isnull(last_seen) OR hours_silent > 24 | table host,hours_silent | sort -hours_silent' -d 'output_mode=json' -d 'exec_mode=oneshot' 'https://<splunk-host>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' | jq '.results | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of sources silent beyond the threshold; target value is 0

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query QRadar's log source management API for sources whose last event timestamp exceeds the defined SLA threshold (24 hours for network, 1 hour for security tools).
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'SEC: <api_token>' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<qradar-host>/api/config/event_sources/log_source_management/log_sources?fields=id,name,type_name,last_event_time,enabled&filter=enabled%3Dtrue' | jq '[.[] | select(.last_event_time < ((now - 86400) * 1000))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of log sources where last_event_time is older than 86400000 milliseconds (24 hours); target is 0

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Sentinel, query the Heartbeat table and cross-reference with configured data connectors to identify agents or sources that have gone silent.
how_to_obtain.command: az monitor log-analytics query -w <workspace-id> --analytics-query 'Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | summarize LastHeartbeat=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer | where LastHeartbeat < ago(1h) | count' --output tsv
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of agents that sent a heartbeat in the past 24 hours but have been silent for more than 1 hour; target is 0

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, open the Data Source Monitoring dashboard (Security > Monitoring > Data Source Monitoring) and filter for sources with 'Stale' or 'No Data' status. In QRadar, go to Admin > Log Source Management and sort by 'Last Event Time' ascending to identify oldest/silent sources. Export or note the count of sources exceeding your defined SLA threshold.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Security > Monitoring > Data Source Monitoring > filter Status=Stale | QRadar: Admin > Log Source Management > sort by Last Event Time | Sentinel: Workbooks > Data Collection Health > Stale Sources tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list or count of sources with no recent data; document each source name and last-seen timestamp; target count is 0

typical_values: 1-5 (minor gaps; typically legacy systems or transient network issues)

option_description: Controls whether SIEM detection rules are stored and managed in a version control system such as Git or SVN, enabling change tracking, rollback to prior states, and a full audit history of rule modifications.
security_impact: The Rego policy for rule_tuning_and_operational_maintainability requires rule_version_control_enabled == true as a mandatory condition in both evaluation paths. Without version control, rule changes cannot be audited, rolled back after faulty deployments, or reviewed in CI/CD pipelines, leading to uncontrolled drift in detection logic and potential loss of effective rules.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM platform's rule management or content management section and look for Git integration, repository settings, or 'Detection as Code' configuration options. In Splunk ES, check Content Management; in Microsoft Sentinel, check the Repositories blade; in Elastic SIEM, check the Rules import/export settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Admin Console > Content Management > Repository / Version Control Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A connected repository URL, branch name, and sync status indicating rules are sourced from or pushed to a VCS.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for a local or remote Git repository containing rule definitions by looking for .git directories or YAML/JSON rule files in known rule staging directories.
how_to_obtain.command: find /opt/siem/rules /etc/siem /var/lib/siem -name '*.yml' -o -name '*.json' | head -20 && git -C /opt/siem/rules status 2>/dev/null || echo 'No git repo found'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'On branch main' or similar git status, confirming rules are tracked in a git repository.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM platform API for repository integration configuration. For Microsoft Sentinel, use the Azure REST API to check workspace source control connections.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<SUB>/resourceGroups/<RG>/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/<WS>/providers/Microsoft.SecurityInsights/sourceControls?api-version=2023-02-01' | jq '.value[].properties.repoType'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing source control integrations with repoType set to 'Github' or 'DevOps', confirming VCS integration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the detection engineering or SOC team to determine whether a documented process exists for committing rule changes to a VCS before or after deployment. Request evidence such as recent pull requests, commit logs, or CI/CD pipeline run history.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation of a written runbook or workflow document referencing Git commits for rule changes, with recent commit history as evidence.

option_description: Defines the maximum number of days permitted between scheduled reviews of active detection rules, during which analysts assess rule efficacy, false positive rates, and continued relevance to the threat landscape.
security_impact: The Rego policy for rule_tuning_and_operational_maintainability requires rule_review_cycle_days <= 90 in its primary evaluation path. Stale rules that go unreviewed accumulate false positives, miss newly relevant attack patterns, and create alert fatigue, degrading the operational value of the SIEM. The acceptable range is 1–730 days, but policy compliance requires 90 days or fewer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the SOC or detection engineering team's documented review schedule, SLA documentation, or runbooks that specify how frequently detection rules are reviewed. Look for calendar invites, recurring ticket templates, or sprint planning artifacts that reference rule review cadence.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented policy or runbook stating a specific review interval (e.g., 'rules reviewed quarterly' = 90 days, 'biannually' = 180 days).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM platform's audit log or rule management history to find the last-modified or last-reviewed timestamps for active rules and calculate the average and maximum gap between reviews.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search 'index=_audit action=rule_update OR action=rule_review | stats max(eval(now()-_time)) as max_days_since_review by rule_name | sort -max_days_since_review | head 20' -auth admin:password
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table showing rule names and the number of days since their last review, with the maximum value representing the effective review cycle.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM rule management interface, sort active detection rules by 'Last Modified' or 'Last Reviewed' date and identify the oldest unreviewed rule. The difference between today and that date represents the upper bound of the review cycle.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Detection Rules > Sort by 'Last Modified' (ascending) > Review oldest rule timestamp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Visibility into the oldest active rule's last-reviewed date, enabling calculation of the actual review cycle duration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the SIEM API to retrieve all active rules with their last-modified timestamps and compute the maximum staleness interval programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://<SIEM_HOST>/api/v1/rules?status=active&fields=id,name,updated_at' | jq '[.rules[] | {name: .name, days_since_update: ((now - (.updated_at | fromdateiso8601)) / 86400 | floor)}] | sort_by(.days_since_update) | reverse | .[0:10]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON array of rules sorted by staleness showing the name and days since last update, with the top entry representing the maximum review gap.

option_description: Describes the maturity level of the process used to validate detection rules before deployment and after tuning changes. Values range from 'none' (no testing), 'manual' (ad-hoc analyst validation), to 'automated' (CI/CD or replay-based testing with synthetic or historical attack data).
security_impact: The Rego policy for rule_tuning_and_operational_maintainability requires rule_testing_process to be in ['manual', 'automated'] for the primary path, or specifically 'automated' for the secondary path that does not require a review cycle constraint. Deploying untested rules risks introducing broken logic, excessive false positives, or silent failures that create undetected detection gaps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the detection engineering team and request documentation of the rule deployment workflow. Ask specifically whether rules are deployed directly to production, validated manually in a staging environment, or run through an automated testing pipeline before activation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A workflow document, deployment checklist, or runbook describing the testing steps. Absence of any documentation indicates 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a CI/CD pipeline is configured for the rule repository in tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, or Azure DevOps. Look for pipeline definitions that include rule validation, sigma conversion testing, or attack simulation replay steps.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub/GitLab Repository > Actions/Pipelines > Review workflow YAML files for rule testing stages
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A pipeline definition file containing stages for rule linting, syntax validation, or attack simulation (e.g., Atomic Red Team, Caldera replay), indicating 'automated'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Look for CI/CD pipeline configuration files in the rule repository that define automated testing workflows.
how_to_obtain.command: find /opt/siem/rules /var/lib/detection-rules -name '.github' -o -name '.gitlab-ci.yml' -o -name 'Jenkinsfile' -o -name 'azure-pipelines.yml' 2>/dev/null | xargs ls -la 2>/dev/null; cat /opt/siem/rules/.github/workflows/*.yml 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'test|validate|replay|atomic'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline configuration file containing test stages referencing rule validation tools (e.g., sigma, pySigma, detection-lab), confirming 'automated' testing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review ticketing system (Jira, ServiceNow) or change management records for evidence of testing steps documented prior to rule deployment. Closed tickets should show a testing sign-off field or QA approval gate.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jira/ServiceNow > Change Management > Filter by 'Detection Rule Deployment' > Review Testing/QA fields
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Change records showing completed testing checkboxes or QA approval steps before rule promotion to production, indicating at least 'manual' maturity.

option_description: Indicates whether obsolete or deprecated detection rules have been formally removed or disabled from the active SIEM ruleset. This prevents alert noise from irrelevant rules, reduces rule sprawl, and ensures the active ruleset reflects the current threat model.
security_impact: The Rego policy for rule_tuning_and_operational_maintainability requires deprecated_rules_removed == true in both evaluation paths. Retaining stale or deprecated rules increases false positive volume, degrades analyst trust in the alert pipeline, and can mask genuinely malicious activity through alert fatigue. Rules with zero alert activity over 180+ days are strong candidates for deprecation review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API to retrieve rules with zero alert activity in the past 180 days or rules explicitly flagged as deprecated, then assess whether any are still in an 'enabled' state.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://<SIEM_HOST>/api/v1/rules?status=enabled' | jq '[.rules[] | select(.last_triggered == null or (.last_triggered | fromdateiso8601) < (now - 15552000))] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of zero, indicating no enabled rules have gone more than 180 days without triggering. Any non-zero count suggests deprecated rules remain active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM rule management interface, filter rules by status 'disabled' or 'deprecated', and verify whether disabled rules have been formally scheduled for removal or are simply toggled off without a deprecation record. Also filter enabled rules by last alert date to identify zero-activity rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Detection Rules > Filter: Status = Disabled OR Deprecated > Review Last Alert Date column > Identify rules with no activity > 180 days
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Either an empty list of deprecated/disabled rules, or a list showing that all deprecated rules have formal removal tickets and none remain enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SIEM platforms with file-based rule storage, search for rule files tagged as deprecated or containing deprecation markers in their metadata.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rli 'deprecated\|obsolete\|status: disabled' /opt/siem/rules/ 2>/dev/null | wc -l; grep -rli 'deprecated\|status: disabled' /opt/siem/rules/ 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l 'enabled: true' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero files matching both 'deprecated' and 'enabled: true', confirming deprecated rules are not active in the ruleset.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the detection team's rule lifecycle management policy or deprecation SOP. Verify whether a formal process exists for identifying, flagging, and removing stale rules on a defined schedule, and whether recent deprecation actions are documented in change logs or ticketing systems.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented deprecation procedure with evidence of recent rule retirement actions (closed tickets, git commits removing rule files, or SIEM audit log entries showing rule deletion).

option_description: Controls whether threat intelligence feed ingestion is actively enabled and configured in the SIEM platform. When enabled, the SIEM receives structured IOC data including malicious IP addresses, file hashes, and domains from external or internal threat intelligence providers.
security_impact: The Rego policy for threat_intelligence_integration requires threat_intel_feeds_enabled == true as a mandatory condition in both evaluation paths. Without active feed ingestion, IOC-based correlation rules cannot function, eliminating the SIEM's ability to detect connections to known malicious infrastructure, reducing detection fidelity for known threat actor TTPs. Default is false, making this a critical activation control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM platform's threat intelligence or feed management configuration panel and verify that the feed ingestion toggle is enabled and at least one feed shows an 'active' or 'connected' status. In Splunk ES, check the Threat Intelligence Management page; in Microsoft Sentinel, check the Threat Intelligence blade; in QRadar, check the X-Force or TAXII feed configuration.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Admin Console > Threat Intelligence > Feed Management > Verify 'Feed Ingestion Enabled' toggle is ON
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Feed ingestion status shows 'Enabled' or 'Active' with at least one feed in a healthy connected state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM platform API to retrieve the threat intelligence configuration and verify that ingestion is enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://<SIEM_HOST>/api/v1/threat-intelligence/config' | jq '{feeds_enabled: .ingestion_enabled, feed_count: (.feeds | length), active_feeds: [.feeds[] | select(.status == "active") | .name]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response showing feeds_enabled: true and at least one entry in active_feeds array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For on-premises SIEM deployments, check the platform configuration files for threat intelligence feed definitions and their enabled status.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'threat_intel|ti_feed|taxii|stix|intel_feed' /etc/siem/config/ /opt/siem/conf/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'enabled\|active\|disabled' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries showing enabled=true or status=active for one or more threat intelligence feed definitions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check SIEM ingestion logs for recent threat intelligence feed update events, which confirm that feed ingestion is active and pulling IOC data.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'threat_intel|ti_feed|ioc_update|feed_sync' /var/log/siem/ingestion.log 2>/dev/null | tail -50 | grep -E 'success|updated|ingested' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent log entries (within the last 24–48 hours) showing successful threat intelligence feed synchronization events with IOC counts.

option_description: Represents the number of threat intelligence feeds currently active and successfully ingesting IOC data (IP addresses, file hashes, domains) into the SIEM. A higher count increases the breadth of known-bad indicator coverage across different threat intelligence sources.
security_impact: The Rego policy for threat_intelligence_integration requires active_feed_count >= 1 in both evaluation paths. Zero active feeds renders threat intel correlation entirely ineffective. While one feed satisfies the policy minimum, mature security programs typically integrate multiple feeds from diverse sources (commercial TI platforms, ISACs, open-source feeds, government feeds) to maximize IOC coverage and reduce blind spots from single-source limitations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM threat intelligence or feed management page and count the feeds displaying a status of 'active', 'connected', or 'healthy'. Exclude feeds showing 'error', 'disconnected', or 'paused' states as these are not actively ingesting data.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Threat Intelligence > Feed Management > Filter by Status = Active/Connected > Count results
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of feeds in active/connected state, e.g., '5 active feeds' representing the current active_feed_count value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API to retrieve all threat intelligence feed configurations and filter for those with an active status, returning the count.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://<SIEM_HOST>/api/v1/threat-intelligence/feeds' | jq '[.feeds[] | select(.status == "active" or .status == "connected")] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the count of currently active feeds, e.g., 3 or 7.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SIEM platforms using TAXII or STIX-based feed configuration files, count the configured and enabled feed entries.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -c 'status.*=.*active\|enabled.*=.*true' /etc/siem/threat_intel/feeds.conf 2>/dev/null || python3 -c "import json; data=json.load(open('/opt/siem/config/ti_feeds.json')); print(sum(1 for f in data['feeds'] if f.get('status') == 'active'))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of active feed entries in the configuration file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM ingestion logs to identify distinct feed sources that have successfully ingested data within the past 24 hours, representing truly active feeds.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'feed_sync_success|ioc_ingested|ti_update' /var/log/siem/threat_intel.log 2>/dev/null | grep "$(date -d '24 hours ago' '+%Y-%m-%d')\|$(date '+%Y-%m-%d')" | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -u | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of distinct feed source identifiers that successfully ingested data in the last 24 hours.

option_description: Represents the operational status of SIEM correlation rules that actively match ingested log events against IOC data from threat intelligence feeds. 'enabled' means all IOC matching rules are active, 'partial' means some are active and some are disabled, and 'disabled' means IOC correlation rules are not running.
security_impact: The Rego policy for threat_intelligence_integration accepts either 'enabled' or 'partial' as satisfying conditions, with 'disabled' causing the countermeasure to fail entirely. Even with active feeds and IOC data ingested, a 'disabled' status means the SIEM is not correlating incoming events against known-bad indicators, nullifying the value of threat intelligence integration. The default is 'disabled', making this a critical activation step.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM correlation rule library and filter for rules that reference threat intelligence lookup tables, IOC lists, or feed-based matching logic. Review each rule's enabled/disabled status and determine whether all, some, or none are active. In Splunk ES, look for correlation searches referencing the 'threat_activity' or 'threat_intel' lookup tables.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console > Detection Rules > Filter by Tags: 'threat-intel' OR 'IOC' OR 'indicator' > Review Enabled/Disabled status of each rule
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All IOC-referencing rules showing 'enabled' (fully enabled), a mix of enabled/disabled (partial), or all showing 'disabled'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API for rules containing IOC lookup references and assess the ratio of enabled to total IOC correlation rules to determine the status classification.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://<SIEM_HOST>/api/v1/rules?tags=threat-intel,ioc' | jq '{total: (.rules | length), enabled: ([.rules[] | select(.enabled == true)] | length), disabled: ([.rules[] | select(.enabled == false)] | length)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON showing total, enabled, and disabled counts. If enabled == total: 'enabled'; if enabled > 0 and disabled > 0: 'partial'; if enabled == 0: 'disabled'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For file-based SIEM rule stores, search for rule files that reference IOC lookup tables or threat intelligence data sources and check their enabled status.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rl 'threat_intel\|ioc_lookup\|ti_feed\|indicator_match' /opt/siem/rules/ 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -l 'enabled: true' 2>/dev/null | wc -l; grep -rl 'threat_intel\|ioc_lookup\|ti_feed' /opt/siem/rules/ 2>/dev/null | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Two counts: first is enabled IOC rules, second is total IOC rules. Equal counts indicate 'enabled'; first count 0 indicates 'disabled'; differing non-zero counts indicate 'partial'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM alert logs for recent IOC-match events to confirm that IOC correlation rules are actively firing and producing alerts, which confirms 'enabled' or at minimum 'partial' status.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'ioc_match|threat_intel_hit|indicator_alert|ti_correlation' /var/log/siem/alerts.log 2>/dev/null | tail -100 | grep "$(date -d '7 days ago' '+%Y-%m-%d')" | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero count of IOC-match alert events in the past 7 days, confirming at least 'partial' IOC correlation rule activity.

option_description: Defines the number of days that historical logs are retained in indexed storage within the SIEM platform, enabling post-incident forensic analysis, retroactive threat hunting against newly discovered IOCs, and evidence preservation for compliance requirements such as PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2.
security_impact: The Rego policy for historical_log_retention_and_forensic_querying requires log_retention_days >= 90 as a baseline condition. Insufficient retention limits the ability to perform forensic investigations for incidents with extended dwell times (industry average exceeding 200 days), prevents retroactive hunting when new IOCs are published, and may violate regulatory compliance mandates that specify minimum retention windows. The valid range is 0–3650 days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM platform's data management, storage, or retention policy settings in the admin console. Look for index retention policies, data lifecycle rules, or storage tier configurations that specify how long indexed log data is kept before archival or deletion.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Admin Console > Data Management > Retention Policies > View indexed storage retention window (days)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A retention policy showing a specific number of days for indexed storage, e.g., '365 days hot storage', '90 days indexed retention'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk deployments, query the index configuration to retrieve the frozenTimePeriodInSecs value (seconds before data is frozen/deleted) and convert to days.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk cmd btool indexes list --debug 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'frozenTimePeriodInSecs|maxTotalDataSizeMB' | head -20; python3 -c "import subprocess; out=subprocess.getoutput(\"splunk cmd btool indexes list | grep frozenTimePeriodInSecs\"); [print(f'{int(v)/86400:.0f} days') for v in [l.split('=')[1].strip() for l in out.splitlines() if '=' in l]]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: frozenTimePeriodInSecs values converted to days (e.g., 7776000 seconds = 90 days, 31536000 seconds = 365 days).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SIEM platform's index or retention configuration file directly to find the retention period definition. File paths vary by platform but commonly include index configuration, data policy, or storage management files.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/siem/config/retention.conf 2>/dev/null || cat /opt/siem/conf/indexes.conf 2>/dev/null || grep -rE 'retention_days|retention_period|hot_buckets|max_age' /etc/siem/ /opt/siem/ 2>/dev/null | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries defining retention_days or equivalent parameter with a numeric value representing the retention window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM platform's administrative API for storage or data management policy settings to retrieve the configured log retention period programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' 'https://<SIEM_HOST>/api/v1/admin/storage/retention' | jq '{retention_days: .hot_storage_retention_days, archive_enabled: .archive_enabled, archive_retention_days: .cold_storage_retention_days}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with retention_days as an integer value, e.g., {retention_days: 365, archive_enabled: true, archive_retention_days: 1095}.

option_description: Controls whether the SIEM or log management platform exposes an active, functioning query interface that allows authorized analysts to search and retrieve historical log data for forensic investigations, threat hunting, and retroactive IOC matching.
security_impact: This attribute is a required condition in the historical_log_retention_and_forensic_querying Rego rule. Without forensic_query_capability_enabled == true, the countermeasure cannot activate regardless of retention period or indexing health. When disabled or broken, analysts lose the ability to perform post-incident investigations, hunt retroactively against newly identified IOCs, and produce compliance-driven evidence—directly extending attacker dwell time by eliminating the forensic reconstruction capability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Execute a bounded historical query against your SIEM via its CLI or REST API targeting data older than 30 days. For Splunk, use the Splunk CLI search command with an earliest/latest time range. A successful response with result rows confirms the capability is enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search 'index=* earliest=-60d@d latest=-30d@d | head 10' -auth admin:$(cat /opt/splunk/etc/passwd_token) -uri https://splunk-host:8089
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON or CSV rows containing log events from the 30-60 day window; non-empty result count confirms forensic query capability is operational.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the SIEM REST API to submit a historical search job and poll for results. For Elastic/OpenSearch, query the _search endpoint with a range filter on @timestamp targeting data older than 30 days.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:${ES_PASSWORD} -X GET 'https://elasticsearch-host:9200/logs-*/_search' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":{"range":{"@timestamp":{"lte":"now-30d"}}},"size":5}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 200 response with hits.total.value >= 1 and populated hits.hits array containing log documents older than 30 days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the SIEM search or investigation interface and manually execute a time-scoped query. In Splunk, open the Search & Reporting app and set the time picker to a custom range beginning 60 days ago and ending 30 days ago. In QRadar, use the Log Activity tab with an Advanced Search filtered to a time window beyond 30 days.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Apps > Search & Reporting > Search bar > Time picker: Custom Range (start: -60d, end: -30d) > Run query 'index=*' | QRadar: Log Activity > Advanced Search > Filter: Start Time = [now-60d], End Time = [now-30d] > Search
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Search results page populates with log events from the specified historical window; absence of 'No results' or timeout errors confirms capability is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SIEM administrator or SOC lead to confirm whether the query interface is operationally maintained and accessible to Tier 1/2 analysts. Verify that no outstanding indexer failures, license overages, or access control misconfigurations are blocking historical searches.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Analyst confirms they can successfully execute historical queries beyond 30 days, and no open tickets indicate broken search functionality or indexer backlog preventing historical data retrieval.

typical_values: true (SIEM search interface is active and historical queries return results)
false (query interface is disabled, misconfigured, license-limited, or search service is down)

option_description: Represents the current operational health of the log indexing pipeline within the SIEM or log management platform. This status reflects whether newly ingested events are being parsed, indexed, and made queryable in a timely manner, or whether the pipeline is degraded, stopped, or in an unknown state.
security_impact: The Rego policy requires log_indexing_status == 'healthy' as a condition for the historical_log_retention_and_forensic_querying countermeasure. A 'degraded' status means recent events may not be searchable, creating detection gaps and compromising forensic timelines. A 'disabled' or 'unknown' status entirely blocks the countermeasure from activating, leaving the organization without reliable indexed log access. In practice, a degraded or disabled indexing pipeline means correlation rules may silently miss events, alerts may not fire, and forensic queries will return incomplete datasets—directly undermining the SIEM's core value during an active incident.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the indexer or ingestion pipeline health directly via CLI. For Splunk, query the introspection endpoint for indexer queue fill ratios and confirm the indexing queue is not backed up. For Elasticsearch, use the cluster health and index stats API to verify shard assignment and indexing throughput.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:${ES_PASSWORD} 'https://elasticsearch-host:9200/_cluster/health?pretty' && curl -sk -u elastic:${ES_PASSWORD} 'https://elasticsearch-host:9200/_nodes/stats/indices/indexing?pretty' | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(n, d['nodes'][n]['indices']['indexing']['index_total']) for n in d['nodes']]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cluster health shows status: green or yellow (not red); index_total values are incrementing across nodes, confirming active indexing. A red cluster status or zero index_total indicates disabled or failed indexing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the SIEM platform's health monitoring or pipeline status dashboard. In Splunk, navigate to Settings > Monitoring Console > Indexing > Indexing Performance to review queue fill percentages and indexing rate. In IBM QRadar, go to Admin > System and License Management > System Health to review log pipeline status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Monitoring Console > Indexing > Indexing Performance (check Indexing Rate and Queue Fill Ratio) | QRadar: Admin tab > System and License Management > System Health View > Log Pipeline Status | Elastic Stack: Kibana > Stack Monitoring > Elasticsearch > Nodes > Indexing Rate graph
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Indexing rate shows a non-zero events-per-second value consistent with expected ingestion volumes; queue fill ratios below 75%; no pipeline pause or error indicators displayed in the dashboard.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SIEM platform's own internal logs for indexing errors, pipeline stalls, or shard allocation failures. For Splunk, review splunkd.log for indexing errors. For Elasticsearch, review elasticsearch.log on each data node for shard allocation exceptions or circuit breaker trips.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'ERROR|WARN' /var/log/elasticsearch/elasticsearch.log | grep -iE 'shard|index|circuit' | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No ERROR lines referencing shard allocation failures, rejected executions, or circuit breaker trips in the last 60 minutes. For Splunk: grep -E 'ERROR|indexer' /opt/splunk/var/log/splunk/splunkd.log | tail -50 returns no critical indexer failures.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM pipeline health API to programmatically retrieve indexing status. For Splunk, poll the services/server/introspection/indexer endpoint. For Elasticsearch, query the _cat/indices API to verify all indices are in 'open' state with green or yellow health and confirm recent index creation timestamps align with expected ingestion.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:${ES_PASSWORD} 'https://elasticsearch-host:9200/_cat/indices?v&h=health,status,index,docs.count,creation.date.string&s=creation.date.string:desc' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All active indices show health=green or health=yellow with status=open; the most recently created index has a creation timestamp within the expected ingestion window (e.g., today's date for daily-rollover indices), confirming the pipeline is actively indexing new data.

typical_values: healthy (indexing pipeline is fully operational, events are being indexed at expected throughput)
degraded (indexing pipeline is running but with errors, backpressure, or partial failures causing delayed or incomplete indexing)
disabled (indexing service is stopped or administratively turned off; no new events are being indexed)
unknown (pipeline health cannot be determined due to missing monitoring, unreachable health endpoints, or incomplete instrumentation)
